newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Refiners profit from Singapore trader buying spree.
newsitem.headline: Refiners profit from Singapore trader buying spree.

text.p: Privately-owned Singapore firm Hin Leong Trading has taken its diesel and jet fuel buying spree to more than US$300 million, giving Asian refiners their best profits in a long time, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"Refinery margins are very good. We must thank him (Hin Leong) for this," one refining source said.
Profits from refining one barrel of Middle East crude at the basic stage reached almost $3.00 late last week compared to a loss of more than $1.00 in January.
The sharp increase in profits was partly due to the near $3.00 per barrel rise in diesel prices in March following Hin Leong's purchase of more than 10 million barrels of diesel.
The jump in diesel prices coincided with a plunge in crude prices as benchmark Brent crude sank to a nine-month low of $17.65 per barrel on Friday.
Hin Leong's trading strategy has completely baffled the Singapore oil market, but at the same time it made many people a lot richer as they cashed in on the soaring prices.
Traders took advantage of the skyrocketing prices by bringing in at least 10 million barrels of diesel from the West to sell to Hin Leong and the regional market.
Singapore prices, at their height in mid-March, were well over $4.00 per barrel higher than those in the West. The difference more than paid for the costs of shipping the fuel east.
May diesel in Singapore is priced now at more than $3.00 per barrel higher than in Europe, leading to more exports from the West, traders said.
Hing Leong declined all comment on its activities, but Despite the large influx of fuel from the West, the company is showing no signs of changing policy, puzzled traders said.
"Does he see a demand that nobody is seeing or does he see a value (for diesel) that nobody is seeing?" one trader asked.
One industry source said Hin leong's large appetite was partly due to the company's failure to renew term diesel purchase contracts with Middle East suppliers.

He said that in the past Hin Leong imported between three to four million barrels of diesel monthly from the Middle East. On Monday, traders said they thought Hin Leong would be winding down its buying frenzy soon because the regional market was not big enough to absorb all the cargoes bought.
But Hin Leong did just the opposite. It bought the largest amount of diesel in one day that anyone in the market could remember for a very long time.
On Tuesday, Hin Leong, together with sister-company Sanko Oil, took the market by storm and bought 1.35 million barrels of diesel and 100,000 barrels of jet fuel.
"I think they (Hin Leong) have no choice. They have to keep buying to maintain prices as they are very long," a trader said.
But other traders said they believed Hin Leong must have an outlet for the fuel as the cost of keeping it unsold in storage would overstretch the company's resources.
